Here’s a look at the annual compensation planning process at Google.

content.text:
## Bottom line

**Negotiate. Don’t accept the initial offer, and don’t walk away yet.**

It’s a **good market-rate L6 offer**, especially in years 1–2, but it is not compelling enough to justify leaving a job you like purely for compensation. On a four-year basis, the offer is only about **5% above your current stated annual compensation**, before assigning any value to Google refresh grants.

If Google does not improve it meaningfully, I would stay at Meta unless the Google role is substantially better for your career or personal interests.

## The economics

Your Google target cash compensation is:

- Base: **$235,000**
- Target bonus: **$47,000**
- Target cash: **$282,000**
- Average initial equity: **$270,000/year**
- Four-year average target compensation: **$552,000/year**

That compares with your current approximately **$526,000**, a difference of only:

- **$26,000/year**
- **4.9%**
- **$104,000 over four years**

That’s a thin premium for:

- Leaving a job you like
- Taking manager, team and reorg risk
- Resetting your reputation and internal network
- Giving up known Meta equity
- Depending on discretionary future refresh grants

Recent self-reported data puts Bay Area Google L6 PM compensation around **$551,000 median**, so the offer is roughly market-median when the initial grant is averaged over four years—not a lowball, but not an exceptional “passive candidate” package either. ([levels.fyi](https://www.levels.fyi/companies/google/salaries/product-manager/locations/san-francisco-bay-area))

### The vesting schedule matters enormously

Before evaluating further, get the exact schedule in writing. Google new-hire grants are commonly reported as front-loaded **38% / 32% / 20% / 10%**, although your actual grant documents control. Refresh grants are generally reported as vesting evenly rather than following that same schedule. ([thesimplemoney.com](https://thesimplemoney.com/employers/google/gsu-grants-and-vesting-schedule))

If your $1.08 million grant uses 38/32/20/10, your target compensation would be:

| Year | Equity vesting* | Target TC |
|---|---:|---:|
| 1 | $410,400 | **$692,400** |
| 2 | $345,600 | **$627,600** |
| 3 | $216,000 | **$498,000** |
| 4 | $108,000 | **$390,000** |
| **4-year average** | $270,000 | **$552,000** |

\*Assumes no stock-price movement.

So this is an excellent **first-two-year offer**, but it has a large years 3–4 cliff. Refresh grants may mitigate that, but Google’s own published compensation-process description says equity refresh amounts depend on factors such as performance, location and role, with manager discretion involved. You should not treat them as guaranteed compensation. ([services.google.com](https://services.google.com/fh/files/blogs/pay_equity_info_sheet.pdf))

Your next-12-month comparison is favorable to Google:

- Meta based on $200,000 vesting: approximately **$476,000**
- Google under 38% first-year vesting: approximately **$692,400**

But that $216,400 first-year advantage is largely front-loading rather than a permanent compensation increase.

## What I would ask for

I would anchor at:

- **Base: $260,000**
- **New-hire RSUs: $1,300,000**
- **Sign-on bonus: $150,000**

That is assertive but defensible:

- $260,000 is still below the posted $271,000 maximum.
- You currently make $240,000 base, so Google is asking you to take a base-pay cut.
- You were recruited rather than actively job hunting.
- You have a strong BATNA: staying in a job you like.
- You are walking away from approximately $200,000 of Meta equity over the next year.
- Google’s refreshes cannot be relied upon.

Tell them you are flexible on the mix: if base is constrained, they can increase equity or sign-on.

### A good landing zone

I would consider the negotiation successful around:

- **$250,000–$255,000 base**
- **$1.20–$1.30 million RSUs**
- **$75,000–$100,000 sign-on**

For example:

- $255,000 base
- $51,000 bonus
- $1.25 million equity
- $100,000 sign-on

That would produce:

- Four-year recurring average before sign-on: **$618,500**
- Four-year average including the sign-on: **$643,500**

That is approximately a **22% four-year premium** over your current $526,000 compensation, which is much more appropriate for leaving a good situation.

They may not improve all three components. Focus on **total four-year value**, not winning every line item.

## Suggested script

> I’m very excited about the team and the opportunity. I also want to be transparent that I’m happy at Meta and wasn’t actively looking, so the compensation needs to make the switching risk worthwhile.
>
> My current annual compensation is approximately $526,000, including about $250,000 per year in equity, and I have approximately $200,000 of Meta equity scheduled to vest over the next 12 months.
>
> At the current offer, the four-year average is about $552,000 before any refresh grants. Since refreshes aren’t guaranteed, that’s only a modest increase over staying, and the proposed base is also below my current $240,000 base.
>
> Could you take back a request for a $260,000 base, $1.3 million new-hire equity grant, and a $150,000 sign-on bonus? I’m flexible on the mix if there are constraints on a particular component, but I need a meaningfully stronger guaranteed package to make the move.

If pressed for a minimum, avoid immediately disclosing it:

> I’m evaluating the package holistically rather than setting an individual minimum for each component. If the team can improve the base, equity and make-whole collectively, I’m confident we can find something that works.

If they ask whether you will sign if they meet the request:

> If we can get close to that package and the remaining details check out, I’d be prepared to make a decision quickly.

Only say that if it is true.

## Questions to settle before accepting

Ask for explicit answers on:

1. **Exact new-hire vesting schedule:** Is it 38/32/20/10, or something else?
2. **First vest date:** When does vesting actually begin?
3. **Grant conversion date:** When is the $1.08 million converted into a fixed number of Alphabet shares?
4. **Refresh eligibility:** Will your start date make you eligible for the next annual refresh cycle, or will you miss or receive a prorated grant?
5. **Typical refresh range:** Ask for the modeled or historical L6 PM refresh for “meets expectations,” even if they cannot promise it.
6. **Bonus proration:** Will your first-year bonus be prorated?
7. **Performance mechanics:** Is the 20% bonus merely a target, and what have typical payouts looked like?
8. **Sign-on repayment:** If added, what is the clawback period?
9. **Level and job code:** Confirm in writing that this is L6 PM, not an adjacent job family with different compensation bands.

The refresh-cycle eligibility question is particularly important: joining shortly after a cutoff could materially reduce your first several years of stacked equity.

## My decision rule

- **At the proposed numbers:** Negotiate; if unchanged, lean **stay at Meta**.
- **At roughly $600,000–$620,000 annualized four-year value, including amortized sign-on:** Reasonable to accept if you prefer the Google role.
- **At approximately $630,000–$650,000:** Strong financial reason to move.
- **Below approximately $590,000:** Probably not enough for a happy, passive candidate unless the role has exceptional career upside.

So: **the offer is good, but not good enough to take without negotiating. Ask for $260K / $1.3M / $150K, aim to land around $255K / $1.25M / $100K, and be willing to stay at Meta if Google will not move meaningfully.**

content.text:
## My recommendation

**I would take it—provided you’re at least reasonably positive about the role, manager, and team.**

The revised package has crossed from “not enough to leave a good situation” to **financially compelling**, although it isn’t an extraordinary L6 offer. If you think the Google role is materially worse than your Meta role, stay. But on compensation alone, I would now favor Google.

## Updated comparison

### Google

- Base: **$240,000**
- Target bonus: **$48,000**
- RSUs: **$1,280,000 over four years**
- Average annual target compensation: **$608,000**
- Four-year total at grant-date stock value: **$2,432,000**

### Meta

Using your stated current compensation:

- Annual compensation: **$526,000**
- Four-year total if sustained: **$2,104,000**

### Difference

Google offers:

- **$82,000 more per year on average**
- **15.6% annual premium**
- **$328,000 more over four years**

That is a legitimate switching premium. It is also essentially in line with the approximately **$606,000 median reported for Bay Area Google L6 PM compensation**, so this is now a solid market offer rather than a lowball. ([levels.fyi](https://www.levels.fyi/companies/google/salaries/product-manager/locations/san-francisco-bay-area?utm_source=openai))

## The vesting schedule is still critical

Confirm the exact schedule in your offer documents. Recent Google offers are often reported as **38% / 32% / 20% / 10%**, but Alphabet’s public filings only confirm that RSUs generally vest over four years—not the precise annual split for your grant. ([sec.gov](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1652044/000165204426000018/goog-20251231.htm?utm_source=openai))

If yours is 38/32/20/10, the compensation profile is:

| Year | Google RSUs | Google target TC | Meta comparison |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | $486,400 | **$774,400** | ~$476,000 based on your next 12-month vest |
| 2 | $409,600 | **$697,600** | ~$526,000 |
| 3 | $256,000 | **$544,000** | ~$526,000 |
| 4 | $128,000 | **$416,000** | ~$526,000 |
| **Average** | **$320,000** | **$608,000** | **~$526,000** |

Under those assumptions, Google pays roughly **$298,400 more during the next 12 months** than staying at Meta.

That means Google has more than economically replaced the $200,000 of Meta shares you’re leaving behind. It did so through additional front-loaded equity rather than a cash sign-on.

The downside is the sharp year-four cliff. Refresh grants are intended to help fill it, but because they aren’t guaranteed, you should make the decision assuming **zero refreshes**. Alphabet itself says RSUs generally depend on continued employment through the applicable vesting date. ([sec.gov](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1652044/000165204426000018/goog-20251231.htm?utm_source=openai))

## Why I now lean “take”

The original offer averaged $552,000, only 5% over Meta. This one averages **$608,000, about 16% over Meta**.

More importantly:

- Google raised the grant by **$200,000**, an 18.5% increase.
- Your base no longer decreases.
- The first two years are likely substantially ahead of Meta.
- Even assuming no Google refreshes and no stock appreciation, the four-year package is approximately $328,000 ahead.
- Any normal Google refreshes would be upside, not necessary to make the initial economics work.
- If you eventually dislike Google, front-loaded vesting may make leaving after two years financially attractive.

The lack of a sign-on is no longer a major problem. A sign-on would be preferable because it is immediate and not exposed to stock-price risk, but the additional $200,000 grant is still real economic value.

## Reasons I would stay at Meta instead

Stay if any of the following are true:

1. **You materially prefer your Meta role or manager.**  
   A 16% average premium may not compensate for going from a great situation to an uncertain or unattractive one.

2. **Your Meta compensation is likely to increase meaningfully.**  
   If a promotion, unusually large refresh, or compensation adjustment is reasonably imminent, $526,000 may understate your actual alternative.

3. **Your Meta equity pipeline beyond the next 12 months is stronger than stated.**  
   Compare all scheduled vesting over four years—not merely the next 12 months.

4. **The Google vesting schedule is not front-loaded.**  
   An even 25% schedule still produces $608,000 annually and remains financially attractive, but it eliminates the unusually strong first-two-year advantage.

5. **You expect to stay at Google for four-plus years but doubt refresh prospects.**  
   At 38/32/20/10, year four falls to approximately $416,000 before refreshes or stock appreciation. You must be comfortable managing that cliff.

6. **The Google role has meaningful layoff, reorganization, commute, scope, or performance risk.**  
   The equity only vests while you remain employed.

## One important apples-to-apples check

Before signing, make a simple spreadsheet with every currently scheduled Meta vest and Google vest by quarter for the next four years.

Do **not** count:

- Future refreshes at either company
- Stock appreciation
- Unvested shares already earned as “lost money” separately from the vesting comparison

Do count:

- Exact vest dates
- Any bonus proration
- Your actual Meta RSU schedule
- Google’s exact vesting percentages
- Any delay between starting and the first Google vest
- Expected target bonus, with an appropriate discount if you doubt target payout

The $200,000 of Meta RSUs is not an additional $200,000 loss on top of staying compensation. It is already captured when you compare Meta’s future vesting with Google’s future vesting. Avoid double-counting it.

## What to do with Meta

I would not reopen negotiations with Google after they explicitly said “best offer,” absent a competing written offer. You got a meaningful improvement.

I also would not solicit a Meta counteroffer unless you are genuinely willing to stay and comfortable with the implications. But before resigning, check whether Meta’s next refresh, compensation review, bonus payment, or vest date is close enough that changing your start date could preserve substantial value.

If there is a vest worth tens of thousands of dollars only a few weeks away, ask Google to move the start date rather than asking for more compensation.

## Final verdict

**Financially: take it.**

**Holistically: take it if the Google opportunity is at least 80–90% as attractive as your current Meta situation.** If you strongly prefer the work, manager, or trajectory at Meta, staying is also rational—the revised offer is strong, but not so overwhelming that you should accept a worse job.

Given that compensation matters a lot to you, my decision would be:

> **Accept the Google offer after confirming the exact vesting schedule, first vest date, and refresh eligibility date.**

At **$608,000 average target compensation and a $328,000 four-year premium before refreshes**, Google is now paying enough to justify the switching risk.
